title: MOS I/V Characteristics
intro: The drain current of a long-channel MOSFET follows a square law above threshold. Almost every first-order analog calculation uses these equations.

blocks.text: Define the overdrive voltage Vov = VGS - VTH. Three regimes matter:

items: Cutoff: VGS < VTH, the channel is off (apart from leakage and subthreshold current).
Triode (linear): VGS > VTH and VDS < Vov. The channel reaches the drain and the device behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor.
Saturation: VGS > VTH and VDS >= Vov. The channel is pinched off at the drain end and the current stops depending (to first order) on VDS. This is where amplifiers are biased.

blocks.source:
Triode:      ID = mu_n*Cox*(W/L) * [ Vov*VDS - VDS^2/2 ]
Saturation:  ID = (1/2)*mu_n*Cox*(W/L) * Vov^2 * (1 + lambda*VDS)
Small VDS:   Ron = 1 / [ mu_n*Cox*(W/L) * Vov ]

blocks.text: The derivation integrates the channel charge per unit length, Qd(x) = W*Cox*(VGS - V(x) - VTH), times the carrier velocity along the channel: ID = W*Cox*(VGS - V(x) - VTH)*mu_n*dV/dx. Integrating from source (V = 0) to drain (V = VDS) over length L yields the triode expression; when VDS reaches Vov the charge at the drain goes to zero, the channel pinches off and the current saturates at the VDS = Vov value.
Transconductance gm = dID/dVGS relates a small change in gate voltage to the change in drain current. In saturation there are three equivalent forms:

They tell different stories: at fixed overdrive gm grows with W/L; at fixed current gm grows only with the square root of W/L; and at fixed W/L, gm is proportional to Vov, while 2*ID/Vov says that to get high gm for little current you want a small overdrive (wide transistors). In the limit Vov tends to 0 the square law fails and weak inversion takes over (see Second-order effects).

Watch where each curve leaves the dashed parabola: that is VDS = Vov, the triode/saturation boundary. In saturation the curves are nearly flat; their slope is set by lambda. Raising VGS lifts the curve with a square-law spacing.

At a fixed W/L, gm only grows as the square root of ID, so doubling the current buys just 41 percent more gm. Doubling W/L instead raises gm by the same factor at fixed current, with no power cost, at the price of more capacitance.

blocks.title: A simple bias point
blocks.text: An NMOS has mu_n*Cox = 200 uA/V^2, W/L = 10, VTH = 0.4 V and lambda = 0. For VGS = 0.8 V and VDS = 1 V find ID and gm. Then find ID for VGS = 0.8 V and VDS = 0.1 V.
solution: Vov = 0.8 - 0.4 = 0.4 V, and VDS = 1 V > Vov so the device is saturated.
With VDS = 0.1 V < Vov the device is in triode: ID = 2 mA/V^2 * (0.4*0.1 - 0.1^2/2) = 2 mA * 0.035 = 70 uA.
blocks.answer: ID = 160 uA, gm = 0.8 mS in saturation; ID = 70 uA at VDS = 0.1 V (triode).
blocks.hint: Check whether VDS is larger than the overdrive voltage first.

blocks.title: Saturation or triode?
blocks.text: A transistor has VG = 1.5 V, VS = 0 V, VD = 1.0 V, VTH = 0.5 V. Which region is it in? What if VD = 0.6 V?
solution: Vov = 1.5 - 0 - 0.5 = 1.0 V. In saturation VDS must be at least Vov.
VD = 1.0 V gives VDS = 1.0 V, exactly Vov: the edge of saturation. VD = 0.6 V gives VDS = 0.6 V < 1.0 V: triode.
blocks.answer: Edge of saturation at VD = 1.0 V; triode at VD = 0.6 V.

blocks.title: What does 2ID/Vov tell you?
blocks.text: Two designs carry the same drain current ID = 100 uA. One uses Vov = 0.2 V, the other Vov = 0.4 V. Compare gm, and say what you pay for the higher one.
solution: gm = 2*ID/Vov. First design: 2*100 uA / 0.2 V = 1 mS. Second: 0.5 mS.

The low-overdrive design has twice the gm for the same current, but needs W/L four times larger (since ID is proportional to (W/L)*Vov^2 at fixed ID, W/L scales as 1/Vov^2). It pays in area and capacitance, and loses voltage headroom margin to stay in saturation.
blocks.answer: 1 mS versus 0.5 mS; the higher gm costs 4x the width (area and capacitance).
